newsitem.title: ITALY: U.N. agency head says famine has hit North Korea.
newsitem.headline: U.N. agency head says famine has hit North Korea.

text.p: The head of the United Nations food aid agency said on Thursday that famine has definitely hit communist North Korea.

"We had been saying in the spring and early summer that this was famine in the making," Catherine Bertini, executive director of the Rome-based World Food Programme (WFP), said in an interview with Reuters.

"But when you see now the pictures of the emaciated children and the bad shape that those children are in, this is famine," she said ahead of a trip to Washington next week where she will appeal for more aid.
Asked if the WFP had any doubts that the situation in North Korea was now in the famine stage, Bertini said: "It is".

International aid workers had said previously that North Korea was on the brink of famine after floods in 1995 and 1996 devastated much of the isolationist country's farmland and industrial bases, exacerbating already severe food shortages.
Pyongyang says severe drought is threatening to do even more damage to its agricultural sector this year.

"In North Korea the food stocks are empty," Bertini said. "The people are literally starving and the only food that's coming in is the food contributed through the international aid effort... There isn't any other food.
"The country's system has run dry and the food that is being distributed is due to the generosity of people all over the world who have come forward with food aid," she said.
The WFP said earlier this month that it had received around 75 percent of the $45.7 million aid it asked for a week before.
Bertini said that every citizen in the world's only remaining Stalinist country potentially risked starvation in the current situation.
"There are 24 million people in the country and every person in the country is reliant on food provided by the government and so all of those people potentially are at risk," she said.
Bertini said a major shortfall of food would continue throughout the country until crops are harvested in the fall.
But she warned that even if the next harvest was good the country would not be out of the woods for some time.
"We understand that the harvest looks reasonably good but it's still not going to be anywhere near enough to feed the people."
She added that it would be a reasonable harvest only if people stay away from it until it is mature.
"If people are so hungry that they go and pick food that is not yet fully grown and fully mature, that, of course would negatively impact the total amount of food available," she said.
"But even if the harvest is full and abundant it will not be enough to provide people with the food for the next year."
Bertini said that children in the hermit East Asian state were now returning to schools after the WFP began a programme of feeding them in the institutions.
"But unfortunately many of these children are emaciated children in very bad shape so the food is absolutely critical to keep them alive," she said.
Bertini appealed for more bilateral aid directly to North Korea and said she was pleased that the United States has announced its first bilateral programme for Pyongyang.

"We cannot tolerate hunger that leads to starvation and we must act with the resources we do have to be sure that that doesn't happen. We can do that with more food, more resources for the people of North Korea now."
